Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Is the movie cop thriller heading for retirement? Colin Farrell, left, and Edward Norton star in "Pride and Glory" as New York cops. It seems incredible to suggest that such a popular form of storytelling might be on the way out, but it's happened before: Musicals and westerns were once staple entertainment for the moviegoing masses, and somewhere in the 1970s they just went thataway. Now the musicals and westerns that emerge are considered unusual. So consider: Last week the top box-office draw in the country was "Max Payne" with Mark Wahlberg as an obsessed cop tracking down the killer who murdered his wife and child. Based on a video game, "Max Payne" takes a rudimentary plot and boils it down still further, to the point where it's worse than predictable. The film's attraction (such as it is) isn't found in story, but in decoration: the blue-filtered chiaroscuro and etch-y comic book compositions, how the snow glints under the streetlights. "Pride and Glory," on the other hand, is resolutely old school. Not only is it not based on a video game, it's hard to imagine that any of the characters has played one -- or seen a movie either.  Watch behind the scenes at "Pride and Glory" » . The time period isn't specified, but it seems to be today, going on 1974. Written by "Tumbleweeds" director Gavin O'Connor and Joe Carnahan ("Narc"), based on a story O'Connor put together with his twin brother Greg and ex-New York cop Robert Hopes, this is one of those movies that wants to emulate the serious side of '70s cinema, to dig into thorny ethical quandaries and alert us to institutional corruption. Unfortunately, it does a poor job. This time Edward Norton is the alienated cop, Ray Tierney. Like Max Payne, he's stepped away from the street to nurse his own grievances -- he bears an ugly scar down his cheek from an incident referred to only obliquely. The details remain hazy, but it casts a "Chinatown"-size cloud over Ray and probably accounts for the state of his marriage -- which is over -- and the fact that he's sleeping on his dad's leaky sailboat. There's considerably more plot in "Pride and Glory" than in "Max Payne," but it's only marginally less predictable. A shooting puts four cops down -- all of them from the command of Ray's brother Francis (Noah Emmerich). Francis is devastated, and the boys' father, Francis Sr. (Jon Voight), insists Ray must step up and take charge of the investigation. The Tierney clan has another cop in the family: Jimmy (Colin Farrell) is married to their sister (Lake Bell). We soon realize Jimmy's hands are dirty. But what will Ray do about it? If you've seen your Sidney Lumet movies -- "Serpico," "Prince of the City," "Q&A" -- then you'll be well ahead of the game. Even if you haven't, you'll have seen the cop shows that drew from them. Which is why almost every scene, every line of dialogue in "Pride and Glory" has the dull thud of cliche. "We can't keep doing this," moans Ray's soon-to-be ex-wife. Any regular moviegoer will know exactly what she means: How many more times will we have to suffer this déja-vu? Granted, originality isn't everything. Last year, James Grey's "We Own the Night" invested a very similar story with subtle character shadings and a subversive edge. What's most disappointing about O'Connor's capably acted but gloomy and portentous movie is how it shies away from any real complexity. The Tierneys may have their faults, but the outsider, Jimmy, is the bad egg (we gather that much when he threatens a baby with a hot iron). When push comes to shove, the brothers do the right thing in a climax so stock you could use it to make gravy. The old school was better than this. And, back then, it wasn't old either. "Pride and Glory" is rated R and runs 129 minutes. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) -- Is the movie cop thriller headed for retirement? Colin Farrell, left, and Edward Norton star in “Pride and Glory” as New York cops.

It may seem incredible to suggest that such a popular form of storytelling could be on its way out, but it has happened before. Musicals and westerns were once staple entertainment for moviegoing audiences, yet somewhere in the 1970s, they simply went thataway. Today, the musicals and westerns that do appear are considered unusual.

Consider this: Last week, the country’s top box-office draw was “Max Payne,” starring Mark Wahlberg as an obsessed cop tracking down the killer who murdered his wife and child. Based on a video game, “Max Payne” takes a rudimentary plot and distills it even further, to the point where it becomes worse than predictable. The film’s attraction, such as it is, lies not in its story but in its visual embellishment: the blue-filtered chiaroscuro, the etched comic-book compositions, and the way the snow glints beneath the streetlights.

“Pride and Glory,” by contrast, is resolutely old school. Not only is it not based on a video game, but it is also difficult to imagine that any of its characters has played one—or even seen a movie. Watch behind the scenes at “Pride and Glory” ».

The time period is not specified, though it appears to be today, verging on 1974. Written by “Tumbleweeds” director Gavin O’Connor and Joe Carnahan (“Narc”), and based on a story O’Connor developed with his twin brother Greg and former New York cop Robert Hopes, this is one of those films that aspires to emulate the serious side of 1970s cinema: to probe thorny ethical dilemmas and expose institutional corruption. Unfortunately, it does so poorly.

This time, Edward Norton plays the alienated cop, Ray Tierney. Like Max Payne, he has stepped away from the street to nurse his own grievances; he bears an ugly scar down his cheek from an incident mentioned only obliquely. The details remain hazy, but the episode casts a “Chinatown”-sized cloud over Ray and likely explains the state of his marriage—which is over—as well as the fact that he is sleeping on his father’s leaky sailboat.

There is considerably more plot in “Pride and Glory” than in “Max Payne,” but it is only marginally less predictable. A shooting leaves four cops dead—all from the command of Ray’s brother, Francis (Noah Emmerich). Francis is devastated, and the brothers’ father, Francis Sr. (Jon Voight), insists that Ray step up and take charge of the investigation.

The Tierney clan has another cop in the family: Jimmy (Colin Farrell), who is married to their sister (Lake Bell). We soon realize Jimmy’s hands are dirty. But what will Ray do about it?

If you have seen your Sidney Lumet films—“Serpico,” “Prince of the City,” “Q&A”—then you will be well ahead of the game. Even if you have not, you will likely have seen the cop shows that drew from them. That is why nearly every scene and every line of dialogue in “Pride and Glory” lands with the dull thud of cliché.

“We can’t keep doing this,” moans Ray’s soon-to-be ex-wife. Any regular moviegoer will know exactly what she means: How many more times must we suffer through this déjà vu?

Granted, originality is not everything. Last year, James Gray’s “We Own the Night” invested a very similar story with subtle character shading and a subversive edge. What is most disappointing about O’Connor’s capably acted but gloomy and portentous film is how it shies away from any real complexity.

The Tierneys may have their faults, but the outsider, Jimmy, is the bad egg—we gather as much when he threatens a baby with a hot iron. When push comes to shove, the brothers do the right thing in a climax so conventional you could use it to make gravy.

The old school was better than this. And back then, it was not old, either.

(CNN) — Could the police thriller be nearing the end of its run as a movie genre?

Colin Farrell and Edward Norton appear in “Pride and Glory” as New York police officers. It may sound odd to wonder whether a once-reliable type of popular film could be fading away, but cinema history has seen this happen before. Musicals and westerns used to be standard fare for mainstream audiences, until sometime in the 1970s they largely disappeared from the center of movie culture. These days, when a new musical or western arrives, it tends to be treated as a rarity.

Consider the previous week’s biggest box-office performer: “Max Payne,” starring Mark Wahlberg as a driven cop searching for the person who killed his wife and child. Adapted from a video game, the movie begins with a basic storyline and strips it down even more, until it becomes not merely foreseeable but worse than that. Whatever appeal the film has lies less in its narrative than in its visual surface: blue-tinted shadows, scratchy comic-book-style framing and the shimmer of snow beneath streetlamps.

“Pride and Glory,” by contrast, is deliberately traditional. It is not adapted from a video game; in fact, it is difficult to picture any of its characters ever having played one — or perhaps even having watched a film. The exact era is never stated, though it appears to be the present day filtered through something like 1974.

The screenplay was written by Gavin O’Connor, director of “Tumbleweeds,” and Joe Carnahan of “Narc.” It is based on a story developed by O’Connor with his twin brother Greg and former New York police officer Robert Hopes. The film clearly aims to follow the more serious strain of 1970s filmmaking, probing difficult moral questions and exposing systemic corruption. Regrettably, it does not succeed very well.

Here, Edward Norton plays the estranged police officer Ray Tierney. Like Max Payne, Ray has withdrawn from active street work while nursing private wounds. A pronounced scar runs down his cheek, the result of some past event referred to only indirectly. The specifics are unclear, but the incident hangs over him in a way reminiscent of “Chinatown,” and it likely helps explain both the collapse of his marriage and his current living arrangement: sleeping aboard his father’s leaking sailboat.

“Pride and Glory” contains far more plot than “Max Payne,” but it is only a little less easy to anticipate. A shooting leaves four officers dead, all of them under the command of Ray’s brother Francis, played by Noah Emmerich. Francis is shattered, while their father, Francis Sr., played by Jon Voight, pushes Ray to return and lead the investigation.

There is another policeman tied to the Tierney family as well: Jimmy, played by Colin Farrell, who is married to their sister, played by Lake Bell. It quickly becomes clear that Jimmy is corrupt. The central question becomes what Ray will do once he understands that.

Anyone familiar with Sidney Lumet’s police-corruption films — “Serpico,” “Prince of the City” or “Q&A” — will be able to predict much of what follows. Even viewers who have not seen those movies have likely watched the television cop dramas that borrowed from them. As a result, nearly every scene and line of dialogue in “Pride and Glory” lands with the flat weight of cliché.

“We can’t keep doing this,” Ray’s soon-to-be ex-wife laments. Regular moviegoers will immediately understand the unintended second meaning: how many more times must audiences sit through this same sensation of déjà vu?

To be fair, novelty is not the only measure of value. The previous year, James Gray’s “We Own the Night” handled a very similar premise with more delicate character work and a sharper, more subversive quality. The greatest disappointment in O’Connor’s film — which is competently performed but grim, heavy and over-serious — is that it avoids genuine ambiguity.

The Tierney family members may be flawed, but Jimmy, the outsider, is clearly presented as the rotten one; that much is obvious when he threatens an infant with a hot iron. And when matters finally come to a head, the brothers make the honorable choice in a finale so formulaic it could be used as stock.

Old-school filmmaking was better than this. And when those earlier films were made, they were not “old school” at all.

“Pride and Glory” is rated R and has a running time of 129 minutes.

counterfactuals.output:
Are cop thrillers going the way of westerns and musicals—once-dominant genres that now appear only sporadically, usually as nostalgia pieces, prestige throwbacks, or half-hearted attempts at revival? Watching *Pride and Glory*, it’s hard not to wonder. The film arrives with all the familiar ingredients of the gritty police drama: a family of cops, a corruption scandal, moral compromise, dimly lit bars, funeral bagpipes, bad men with badges, and anguished speeches about loyalty. Yet instead of revitalizing the genre, it seems trapped inside it, dutifully repeating conventions without finding a fresh reason for them to exist.

What makes *Pride and Glory* especially frustrating is that it clearly wants to be taken seriously. This is not a pulpy, stylized action vehicle like *Max Payne*, which at least embraces its comic-book gloom, noir exaggeration, and video-game DNA. *Max Payne* may be messy, shallow, and absurd, but it knows it is operating in a heightened universe of snow, shadows, demons, and revenge-fantasy brooding. *Pride and Glory*, by contrast, strains for authenticity and moral weight. It wants to be *Serpico*, *Prince of the City*, *The Departed*, and a tragic family melodrama all at once. But the harder it pushes toward importance, the more generic it feels.

The plot centers on the Tierney family, an Irish-American clan deeply embedded in the NYPD. Edward Norton plays Ray Tierney, the haunted good cop pulled into an investigation after several officers are killed in an ambush. Colin Farrell plays Jimmy Egan, Ray’s brother-in-law and a cop whose swagger and volatility immediately announce that he is not merely bending rules but snapping them in half. Jon Voight appears as the family patriarch, a high-ranking officer with a heavy conscience and a fondness for gravelly speeches. Noah Emmerich plays Ray’s brother Francis, another cop caught between institutional pressure, family loyalty, and the widening corruption scandal.

On paper, that is a strong cast and a sturdy setup. In execution, the film reduces nearly everyone to a type. Norton, usually one of the most intellectually alert actors in American movies, spends much of the film looking pained and principled in a muted, underwritten role. Ray is supposed to be the moral center, but he often feels more like a narrative device: the man who asks questions, stares at evidence, and reacts with wounded disbelief as the rot spreads closer to home. Farrell fares slightly better because Jimmy is the showier part, but the performance leans hard into sweaty menace and overcompensating machismo. He is dangerous, yes, but rarely surprising. Voight’s patriarch, meanwhile, is burdened with the kind of dialogue that sounds less like a person speaking than a screenwriter underlining the theme: family, honor, the badge, the job, the price of silence.

The film’s biggest problem is not that it is poorly made in a basic technical sense. Gavin O’Connor directs with a certain muscular competence. The streets are gray, the interiors are cramped, the precincts feel worn down, and the violence has an ugly bluntness. But competence is not the same as urgency. *Pride and Glory* is so committed to being grim that it forgets to be compelling. Scene after scene arrives with the same sour intensity, the same clenched-jaw seriousness, the same visual palette of institutional decay. There is little modulation, little tension-building, and almost no sense of discovery. From early on, the film points toward corruption, betrayal, and family implosion, then trudges there exactly as expected.

Compared with *Max Payne*, *Pride and Glory* is certainly more respectable, but not necessarily more alive. *Max Payne* is a flawed genre exercise that fails through excess; *Pride and Glory* fails through weight. *Max Payne* throws supernatural imagery and noir affectation at the wall, sometimes laughably, but at least it has a visual identity. *Pride and Glory* has realism, but it is the kind of realism that has been processed through dozens of previous police dramas. The handheld camera, the blue-gray city, the angry interrogations, the compromised narcotics unit, the family dinner full of buried resentments—all of it feels secondhand.

The screenplay is particularly disappointing because it treats moral complexity as though it can be achieved simply by putting good people in bad institutions and bad people at family gatherings. But real complexity requires more than proximity. The film tells us that loyalty to family and loyalty to the law are in conflict, yet it rarely makes that conflict feel genuinely agonizing. Characters conceal things because the plot requires them to. They explode because the genre requires them to. They drink, shout, bleed, and confess, but their anguish often feels prefabricated.

There are moments when *Pride and Glory* threatens to become a sharper, nastier movie. A few scenes involving Farrell’s character reveal the true horror of a corrupt cop: not merely that he breaks the law, but that he carries the authority of the law into every room he terrorizes. Those scenes have a brutal charge, and they suggest a film willing to stare directly at the abuse of power. But even there, *Pride and Glory* tends to mistake shock for insight. It shows corruption as monstrous, but not especially systemic. The focus remains on individual guilt and family shame rather than a deeper examination of how such behavior survives, spreads, and gets protected.

The family-drama angle is also oddly inert. The Tierneys are meant to represent a dynasty corroded from within, but the relationships are sketched too broadly to hurt as much as they should. The men share history, resentment, and obligation, but the film rarely gives those bonds texture beyond exposition and confrontation. When the emotional reckoning finally arrives, it feels less like tragedy than inevitability. The film has been announcing its seriousness for so long that the climax lands with a thud rather than a punch.

At over two hours, *Pride and Glory* also feels bloated. Its pacing is heavy, and its structure lacks momentum. Investigative scenes blur into domestic confrontations, which blur into cover-ups, which blur into more scenes of men looking devastated in low light. There is a potentially lean, nasty 100-minute thriller buried somewhere inside this material, but the finished film is too enamored of its own solemnity to move with any real force.

The shame is that the ingredients are not bad. Norton, Farrell, Voight, and Emmerich are capable actors. The premise has built-in tension. The subject—police corruption within a family devoted to the police—is rich with dramatic possibility. But *Pride and Glory* never escapes the shadow of better films. It is too conventional to be revelatory, too self-serious to be entertaining, and too dramatically blunt to be tragic.

If *Max Payne* represents one dead end for the modern crime thriller—empty style, artificial darkness, and video-game brooding—then *Pride and Glory* represents another: prestige grit without freshness, moral seriousness without depth, and genre familiarity without pleasure. One film is cartoonishly overblown; the other is oppressively earnest. Neither makes a strong case for the health of the genre, but *Pride and Glory* is the more disappointing because it believes it is doing something substantial.

In the end, *Pride and Glory* is a cop thriller that arrives late to its own funeral. It wears the uniform, knows the rituals, and speaks the language, but the life has gone out of it. For a film about compromised institutions and broken codes of honor, its greatest failure is artistic: it follows every rule of the gritty police drama and still comes away feeling hollow.

# Review: *Pride and Glory* — A Gritty Cop Drama That Wears Its Influences on Its Sleeve

In *Pride and Glory*, director Gavin O’Connor delivers a brooding, blood-soaked police drama about family loyalty, institutional rot, and the moral cost of looking the other way. Starring Edward Norton, Colin Farrell, Jon Voight, and Noah Emmerich, the film aims for the muscular intensity of classic New York corruption thrillers, but while it has committed performances and a grim atmosphere, it often gets weighed down by familiar genre clichés.

## Plot Summary

The story centers on the Tierney family, a clan deeply embedded in the New York Police Department. Ray Tierney, played by Edward Norton, is a once-promising detective who has retreated from the front lines after a professional and personal crisis. He is pulled back into a major investigation after four officers are killed in a drug-related ambush.

The case quickly becomes complicated when Ray discovers that the slain officers may have been involved in corruption — and that the trail leads uncomfortably close to his own family. His brother, Francis Tierney Jr. (Noah Emmerich), commands the precinct under scrutiny, while his brother-in-law, Jimmy Egan (Colin Farrell), is a hotheaded cop whose methods are increasingly difficult to defend.

At the top of the family is Francis Tierney Sr., played by Jon Voight, a veteran NYPD official who believes fiercely in the department and in family loyalty. As Ray digs deeper, he is forced to choose between protecting the family name and exposing the truth.

## Cast and Performances

Edward Norton brings a subdued, haunted quality to Ray Tierney. His performance is less explosive than some of his best-known work, but he effectively conveys a man worn down by guilt and disillusionment. Ray is the moral center of the story, though the script sometimes makes him more of a symbol of conscience than a fully surprising character.

Colin Farrell has the showier role as Jimmy Egan, a corrupt and volatile officer whose charisma masks cruelty and desperation. Farrell leans into Jimmy’s menace, giving the film its most unpredictable energy. Even when the writing pushes him toward stereotype, Farrell keeps the character watchable.

Jon Voight delivers a heavy, old-school performance as the family patriarch, a man who has spent a lifetime confusing loyalty with justice. Noah Emmerich is strong as Francis Jr., caught between command responsibility, family pressure, and denial. The supporting cast, including Jennifer Ehle and Lake Bell, adds emotional texture, though the film’s female characters are mostly pushed to the margins.

## A Throwback to 1970s Police Corruption Films

*Pride and Glory* clearly draws inspiration from the gritty police dramas of the 1970s, a period when American cinema was fascinated by compromised institutions and morally exhausted lawmen. Films like *Serpico* and *The French Connection* helped define the image of New York as a place where the line between cop and criminal could blur under pressure.

There are also echoes of *Prince of the City*, Sidney Lumet’s sprawling examination of police corruption and personal betrayal. Like Lumet’s work, *Pride and Glory* is interested in the culture of silence inside law enforcement — the idea that brotherhood can become a shield for brutality and criminality.

The film’s grim lighting, tense precinct scenes, family confrontations, and urban paranoia all feel designed to evoke that era. It wants to be a modern heir to those morally complex dramas, where justice is messy and institutions are deeply compromised.

## The Problem: Too Many Familiar Moves

For all its ambition, *Pride and Glory* struggles with predictability. The film is packed with recognizable elements: the good cop with a wounded past, the corrupt cop who has gone too far, the family dinner loaded with tension, the patriarch demanding loyalty, and the climactic moral reckoning.

These clichés are not fatal on their own — many great crime films rely on familiar structures — but *Pride and Glory* often presents them without enough freshness. The dialogue can feel overly blunt, especially when characters debate honor, loyalty, and corruption in ways that underline the themes too heavily.

The movie also leans hard into macho anguish. Men shout in kitchens, drink in bars, bleed in alleys, and wrestle with codes of silence. That atmosphere fits the genre, but it sometimes makes the film feel like a compilation of scenes from earlier, better police dramas rather than a reinvention of them.

## Final Verdict

*Pride and Glory* is a serious, well-acted crime drama with a strong cast and a clear affection for the classic police corruption films of the 1970s. Edward Norton gives the story a steady moral gravity, while Colin Farrell adds danger and intensity. The film’s themes — family, loyalty, corruption, and justice — are compelling, and its gritty New York setting gives it weight.

But the movie never fully escapes the shadow of its influences. It wants to stand alongside films like *Serpico*, *The French Connection*, and *Prince of the City*, yet too often settles for familiar genre beats and overwrought family drama.

For fans of dark cop thrillers, *Pride and Glory* is worth watching for its performances and atmosphere. But as a police corruption saga, it is more respectable than remarkable — a film with plenty of grit, but not enough originality.

**‘Pride and Glory’ digs into a familiar blue wall of silence**

*Archived movie review — 2008*

“Pride and Glory” arrives as a somber, hard-edged police-family drama, the kind of New York corruption story built on loyalty, blood ties and the slow realization that doing the right thing may mean destroying the people closest to you.

The film stars **Edward Norton** as Ray Tierney, a damaged NYPD detective pulled back into an investigation after four officers are killed in a drug raid gone wrong. **Colin Farrell** plays Jimmy Egan, a volatile cop whose charm masks a brutal moral collapse. **Jon Voight** is the family patriarch, a high-ranking police official steeped in departmental tradition, while **Noah Emmerich** plays Ray’s brother, a precinct commander caught between duty and family allegiance.

Directed by **Gavin O’Connor**, “Pride and Glory” is less a mystery than a grim march toward exposure. The movie’s pleasures are in the performances and the atmosphere: dim bars, tense squad rooms, grieving widows and cops who speak in half-truths because the full truth would blow their lives apart.

As police dramas go, this is sturdy, muscular material — but also familiar. The film walks territory already mapped by classics such as **“Serpico,”** with its portrait of one officer confronting systemic corruption, though “Pride and Glory” lacks that film’s lean urgency and sense of discovery. It also invites comparison to **“We Own the Night,”** another recent New York crime drama about family, law enforcement and divided loyalties. Where “We Own the Night” leaned into melodrama and nightclub-era atmosphere, “Pride and Glory” is heavier, grayer and more procedural.

Norton gives the film its conscience, underplaying Ray as a man who has already seen too much. Farrell, meanwhile, brings dangerous energy to Jimmy, making him less a simple villain than a man who long ago learned how to justify the unforgivable. Voight adds old-guard weight, though the family-dynasty elements occasionally push the movie toward operatic cliché.

The problem is that “Pride and Glory” often feels like a very serious version of a story moviegoers have seen before. The corruption is ugly, the betrayals are painful, and the moral choices are stark — but the film rarely surprises. Its length and brooding tone can make it feel overburdened, even when individual scenes land with force.

Still, for viewers drawn to bleak cop dramas, “Pride and Glory” offers solid acting, a convincing sense of institutional rot and enough emotional friction to hold attention.

**Rating:** R, for strong violence, pervasive language and brief drug content.  
**Genre:** Crime drama / police thriller.  
**Running time:** About 2 hours, 10 minutes.  
**Bottom line:** A well-acted but overly familiar police-corruption drama, stronger in performance than in originality.
